title: API, command line and agent access
desc: A documented REST API with a machine readable specification, a command line that prints JSON, an agent protocol server, and webhooks for everything the platform does.
h1: Every capability is an interface first, and a screen second
standfirst: There is nothing you can do in the console that you cannot do over the API. That is a design rule rather than an aspiration, and it is what allows an agent to run real work here instead of describing it.

sections.title: The four ways in
sections.lede: Pick the one that fits, or use all of them. They reach the same records under the same permissions.

items.title: The REST API
items.text: Every module exposes its operations over HTTP with JSON in and JSON out. A machine readable specification is published, so a client can be generated rather than hand written, and an agent can discover the available operations without being told about them.
items: A published specification describing every operation and its rules
Consistent conventions for filtering, pagination and errors
Credentials are never returned, including in responses that would otherwise echo them

items.title: The command line
items.text: One binary that talks to the same API and prints JSON, which means it pipes into another tool or straight into a script. It includes generic call and post commands, so a new endpoint is usable before a typed wrapper exists.
items: Around forty commands covering the whole platform
A generic call and post for anything not yet wrapped

items.title: The agent protocol server
items.text: A server that presents the platform to an agent client as a set of callable tools over a standard protocol. It runs as a local process the client launches, holds no state of its own, and authenticates with the same scoped key.
items: Point any compatible agent client at it with two settings
Each tool maps to an API operation with typed arguments and a description
Permissions come from the key, so the tool list is the permission list

items.title: Webhooks and callbacks
items.text: The platform receives events from carriers and providers, verifies them, and acts on them. Outbound notification for your own integrations follows the same model, so an external system can be told when work changes rather than polling for it.

sections.title: A request, and what comes back
sections.lede: Authenticate with a scoped key and ask for identity. Everything else follows the same shape.

sections.title: The same thing from the command line
sections.lede: JSON out, so it composes. The last two commands reach any endpoint, including ones that do not have a typed command yet.
sections.text:
export ALPHAFLUX_API_KEY=afx_...
export ALPHAFLUX_BASE=https://alphaflux.net

alphaflux me
alphaflux field jobs add --customer "Acme LLC" --service "Treatment" --date 2026-10-02
alphaflux field status --id fs_job:abc123 --status done
alphaflux phone text --to +15095551234 --body "On the way"
alphaflux billing run
alphaflux key create --label dispatch-agent --scopes "field:write,phone:read"

alphaflux call api/dashboard
alphaflux post api/notes --json '{"account":"fieldroutes:10000","body":"Called back, no answer"}'

sections.title: How keys and scopes work
sections.lede: An integration is a credential with a job to do. Nothing about the design assumes a human holds it.

items.title: Scoped read and write
items.text: Access is granted per module, so an integration that books work does not need the billing module and does not get it.

items.title: Hashed and shown once
items.text: A key is displayed at the moment it is created and stored only as a hash. Losing one means issuing a new one, not recovering the old one.

items.title: Inherits its owner
items.text: A key carries exactly the permissions and companies of the account that created it, and cannot reach past them.

items.title: Revocable immediately
items.text: Disable a key and every request using it stops. Nothing else on the account is disturbed.

items.title: Optional expiry
items.text: A key can be issued with an expiry date for temporary or contractor access.

items.title: Every use is recorded
items.text: Actions are written to the audit trail against the account that owns the key, so a key is never anonymous.

sections.title: Why the platform was built this way
body: Most business software treats its API as a concession. It exists, it lags the interface, and some things are simply not exposed. That is no longer a defensible position now that a meaningful share of work is done by software talking to software.

The rule here is the opposite. A capability is designed as an interface first and then wrapped in a screen. The screen is a client. The command line is a client. An agent is a client. If something is missing from one of them, it is a bug rather than a decision.

It also future proofs the work. When an operation is available over a documented interface with a machine readable specification, the next tool that needs it does not require anyone's permission or a new integration project. It reads the specification and does the work.

And it means the audit trail is complete. An agent, a script, a scheduled job and a person all arrive through the same door, so every change is attributable to something identifiable rather than to root.

sections.title: What each plan includes
rows: Your own API surface for your customers

faq.a: Yes. A test company can be created alongside the real one with its own records and its own keys, so an integration can be built and broken without touching live data.

Requests are rate limited per key to protect the platform, and the limit is generous enough that a normal integration never meets it. The response headers tell you where you are against the limit rather than leaving you to discover it by being refused.

faq.q: What happens if an integration breaks something?
faq.a: Everything it did is attributed to its key and visible in the audit trail, and the key can be disabled immediately. Financial records are voided rather than deleted and merges are reversible, so a bad batch can be walked back.

faq.q: Can I use an agent client that is not yours?
faq.a: Yes. The agent server speaks a standard protocol, so any compatible client can use it. There is nothing proprietary about the connection, and the key is the only thing that decides what the agent can reach.

faq.q: Can I build my own product on top of this?
faq.a: That is what white label is for. It gives you the platform under your own brand with resale rights, and the same interfaces to build against.
